classification.difficultyReason: Requires combining domain exclusions, signed limits, turning-point reciprocation and reversed monotonicity. Part a includes distinguishing a reciprocal hole from a vertical asymptote, but the necessary reasoning follows the supplied teaching directly.

content.prompt: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is given. Sketch $y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

answer.worked:
Write $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. Preserve the original domain: $(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)$.

As $x\to0^+$, $f(x)\to0^-$, so $g(x)\to-\infty$ and $x=0$ is a vertical asymptote. As $x\to1^-$, $f(x)\to-\infty$ and $g(x)\to0^-$. As $x\to1^+$, $f(x)\to+\infty$ and $g(x)\to0^+$. Keep an open circle at $(1,0)$ because $f$ is undefined at $x=1$.

The minimum of $f$ at $(2,1)$ becomes a maximum of $g$ at $(2,1)$. Reverse increasing and decreasing behaviour on each branch. As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to\infty$ and $g(x)\to0^+$, giving horizontal asymptote $y=0$.

answer.worked:
Write $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The point $(0,\tfrac12)$ becomes $(0,2)$, a minimum. The exclusions $x=-1$ and $x=1$ remain.

Near each excluded point, $f(x)$ tends to zero. Thus $x=-1$ and $x=1$ are vertical asymptotes:
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&\to-\infty &&\text{as }x\to-1^-\\g(x)&\to+\infty &&\text{as }x\to-1^+\\g(x)&\to+\infty &&\text{as }x\to1^-\\g(x)&\to-\infty &&\text{as }x\to1^+.\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $g$ matches the sign of $f$: positive between the asymptotes and negative outside them. Reverse increasing and decreasing behaviour on each interval. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $f(x)\to-\infty$, so $g(x)\to0^-$. Draw the two outer branches approaching horizontal asymptote $y=0$ from below.

spec.description: Complete reciprocal sketch with vertical asymptotes at x=-1 and x=1, a positive central branch with minimum (0,2), and negative outer branches approaching y=0.
spec.mathematics: Qualitative reciprocal sketch using the given signs, limiting behaviour and turning point; no equation is asserted. The original exclusions remain at the vertical asymptotes.
